title: What Is the Gospel
core: The gospel is the good news of God’s saving reign made known in Jesus Christ: he died for our sins, was buried, was raised, and is Lord. It calls people to repent, trust him, and become his disciples.
why: A newcomer needs the central announcement before a catalogue of controversies. This study also helps experienced readers distinguish the saving message from a promise of prosperity, a political program, or a technique for becoming a better person.

scripture.note: Jesus announces God’s kingdom and calls for repentance and belief.
Paul summarizes Christ’s death for sins, burial, resurrection, and appearances.
Confession of Jesus as Lord and belief in his resurrection accompany the promise of salvation.
God makes sinners alive by grace and creates them for good works.

explicit: Paul says the message he received and passed on concerns Christ’s death for sins and resurrection, both according to the Scriptures. Ephesians places God’s mercy before the believer’s transformed conduct. Mark joins the announcement of the kingdom to a call for response.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: kingdom proclamation and the cross-resurrection announcement belong together. The identity of the crucified and risen king explains both what God has done and the allegiance his good news invites. Luke 24:44-49 joins suffering, resurrection, forgiveness, and worldwide witness.
unnoticed: Paul’s concise gospel summary includes named witnesses and his own former persecution; the message is attached to events and transformed relationships, not simply timeless advice.
context: No outside historical claim is necessary for the central definition. Questions about historical investigation of the resurrection belong beside the biblical testimony, identified as a distinct inquiry.
visual: Create an opening path with four linked scenes: promise, cross, resurrection, and response. Each scene displays its passage in context; a final panel connects grace to discipleship without suggesting that deeds purchase salvation.
caveats: Christian traditions differ about how baptism, justification, and perseverance fit into receiving salvation. Do not hide those differences, but do not make a complete theory of salvation a prerequisite for understanding this announcement. Scripture does not prescribe one mandatory wording of a conversion prayer.
questions: What has God done?
What does trusting Jesus involve?
How do grace and obedience fit together?

title: Knowing the God Who Makes Himself Known
core: The Bible presents God as the living Creator who speaks, acts, judges, saves, and enters covenant relationship. His attributes describe the same God from different angles: faithful, wise, holy, loving, just, and unlimited in power and knowledge.
why: This provides a starting vocabulary for theology. Readers can move from vague ideas about a higher power to the specific character and actions the biblical writers describe, while recognizing the limits of human understanding.

scripture.note: God identifies himself to Moses and commits to deliver Israel.
God proclaims mercy, faithfulness, forgiveness, and justice.
Contrasts God’s enduring existence with human frailty.
Celebrates God’s knowledge and presence.
Distinguishes the Creator from idols and summons people to repentance.

explicit: God is not dependent on human service for life. Exodus presents him as attentive to oppression and faithful to the ancestors. The psalms affirm that human concealment and mortality do not limit him.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: the attributes must be read together. Exodus 34 refuses to separate mercy from moral seriousness. Acts 17 connects God’s transcendence with his nearness, then moves toward judgment through the appointed risen man.
unnoticed: Moses receives the revelation of God’s name in the context of a rescue commission; knowing God leads immediately to responsibility toward suffering people.
context: Terms such as omniscience, omnipotence, and aseity are later theological shorthand for scriptural claims, not words whose mere presence proves a doctrine. This page defines the concepts through passages rather than philosophical vocabulary alone.
visual: Build an attribute map whose nodes contain complete passage units. Selecting "faithful" highlights covenant actions; selecting "holy" highlights both worship and ethical demands. Use overlapping links, avoiding a diagram that divides God into separate parts.
caveats: Anthropomorphic language about God’s hand, face, or regret requires genre and context. God’s power does not mean that contradictions become meaningful: Titus 1:2 says God does not lie. A doctrinal summary cannot exhaust the God it describes.
questions: How can God be known without being fully comprehended?
Which attributes describe his actions toward people?

title: Holiness and the Nearness of God
core: God’s holiness is his incomparable purity and majesty. The holy God calls his people to belong to him and to reflect his character in worship, justice, truthfulness, and care for neighbors.
why: Holiness is often reduced either to frightening distance or to a list of private restrictions. Reading worship and conduct together shows why God’s presence is both a gift and a summons to transformed life.

scripture.note: God’s holiness exposes sin, provides cleansing, and leads to commission.
Israel’s holiness includes economic honesty and love of neighbor.
The call to holiness is applied to believers redeemed through Christ.
Joins pursuit of holiness with grateful, reverent worship.

explicit: Isaiah confesses unclean lips, receives cleansing, and responds to God’s call. Leviticus prohibits exploitation of workers and partiality in judgment within its holiness instructions. Peter calls believers to holy conduct grounded in redemption.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: holiness has a relational and ethical shape. Separation for God is directed toward faithful life among others, not self-protective contempt for outsiders. Isaiah’s sequence is encounter, cleansing, and service, rather than self-purification followed by an earned encounter.
unnoticed: The same Leviticus chapter that commands holiness forbids withholding a laborer’s wages overnight. Economic conduct belongs in the holiness discussion.
context: No archaeological explanation is needed. Ritual purity rules and moral wrongdoing must not be treated as identical categories; Leviticus can describe ordinary bodily conditions as ritually unclean without calling them sins.
visual: Pair an Isaiah encounter diagram with a Leviticus daily-life map. Selecting cleansing, speech, work, or neighbor opens the relevant verses and a related New Testament passage.
caveats: Christians disagree about how Israel’s ritual boundaries apply after Christ, but 1 Peter explicitly retains the call to holiness. Do not turn Isaiah’s individual vision into a compulsory emotional sequence for every conversion. Reverence does not authorize cruelty toward people deemed impure.
questions: Why does holiness affect both worship and money?
What is the difference between ritual impurity and sin?

title: Love That Acts Before It Is Returned
core: God’s love is shown in his faithful concern and saving action, supremely in giving his Son for sinners. Christian love answers that gift through concrete care, truthfulness, generosity, and love of enemies.
why: Love can become a vague feeling detached from the cross or from moral responsibility. This study shows the shape Scripture gives it and equips readers to connect doctrine with treatment of real people.

scripture.note: God’s love and covenant faithfulness precede Israel’s greatness or achievement.
God’s giving of the Son is set beside belief, light, and judgment.
Christ dies for the ungodly and reconciles enemies.
God’s initiating love grounds mutual love and confidence before judgment.
The Father’s generosity grounds love of enemies.

explicit: God loved Israel without choosing it for numerical greatness. Christ died for sinners rather than waiting for them to become worthy. First John says that love for God cannot be detached from love for a visible brother or sister.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: love is not the opposite of holiness or justice. John 3 places the gift of the Son in a passage about light exposing evil. God’s love creates the possibility of repentance; it does not rename evil as good.
unnoticed: First John’s argument moves from the unseen God to the neighbor one can see: the credibility of a claimed love for God is tested in ordinary relationships.
context: No original-language claim is needed to establish the point. A later Greek word study should not claim that one Greek word automatically guarantees a uniquely divine kind of love in every occurrence.
visual: Use a Scripture network centered on divine initiative. Draw outgoing links to enemy love, generosity, forgiveness, and truthful conduct; distinguish each passage’s immediate audience and setting.
caveats: Christian traditions debate the scope and application of atonement and final judgment. Those debates should not obscure the explicit command to love enemies. Loving someone does not require endorsing every action or abandoning truthful accountability.
questions: How is love more than feeling?
Does judgment contradict love?
What does loving an enemy look like?

title: Justice Mercy and the Wrath of God
core: God judges evil impartially, protects the vulnerable, and offers mercy. Biblical wrath describes his opposition to wrongdoing; it should be studied with his patience, his concern for victims, and his call to repentance.
why: This prevents a division between an angry Old Testament God and a loving New Testament God. It also guards against treating divine judgment as permission for personal revenge or communal hatred.

scripture.note: Names mercy and moral accountability together.
God’s impartiality includes justice for orphan, widow, and foreigner.
Warns the self-righteous judge and affirms impartial judgment.
Forbids private revenge and commands practical kindness to enemies.
Connects patience, repentance, judgment, and new creation.

explicit: God shows no partiality. Romans tells readers that judging others does not exempt them from judgment. The same letter entrusts vengeance to God and commands believers to feed hungry enemies.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: hope in divine justice can release believers from revenge rather than intensify it. Mercy is not indifference to victims; judgment is not a divine version of uncontrolled human irritation. Scripture presents God’s patience as morally purposeful.
unnoticed: Romans 12 places leaving vengeance to God immediately beside feeding an enemy. A doctrine of judgment is meant to change behavior toward opponents.
context: No external historical explanation is required for the main claims. Theological terms such as retributive and restorative can help compare theories but should be introduced as analytical categories, not biblical labels.
visual: Create a comparison table with wrongdoing, threatened judgment, patience, response, and restoration in selected passages. Keep the invitation to self-examination visible so the page cannot function only as a chart of other people’s guilt.
caveats: The meaning and duration of final punishment are disputed elsewhere in this library. Do not settle them by one metaphor. Collective judgments in ancient narratives require attention to their specific covenant setting and do not license modern violence against an ethnic or religious group.
questions: Why does Scripture speak about wrath?
How can justice protect victims while forbidding revenge?

title: Providence and Responsible Human Action
core: Providence is God’s sustaining and governing care over creation and history. Scripture also portrays people as responsible agents whose choices can be evil, faithful, wise, or foolish.
why: Readers need a framework for praying, planning, and enduring suffering without pretending to know why every event occurred. This study keeps trust in God alongside moral responsibility and practical action.

scripture.note: Joseph distinguishes his brothers' evil intent from God’s good purpose.
Places human planning under God’s direction.
Grounds freedom from anxious striving in the Father’s care.
Holds divine purpose and human responsibility together in Jesus' death.
Calls planners to humility about the future.

explicit: Joseph does not call his brothers' betrayal good; he names its evil intention while affirming God’s saving purpose. Acts likewise calls Jesus' execution lawless while describing it within God’s plan. James criticizes boastful certainty about tomorrow.
insight: Debated interpretation: Reformed accounts often describe God’s decree as compatible with responsible human willing; Arminian accounts emphasize grace-enabled freedom that can resist God. Both must explain the conjunction in Genesis 50 and Acts 2 rather than deleting either side.
unnoticed: Joseph’s confidence leads him to provide food for the very family that harmed him. His statement about providence has an immediate reconciliatory consequence.
context: Historical theology: Westminster Confession chapters 3 and 5 systematize divine decree and secondary causes; Wesley’s Free Grace argues against unconditional reprobation. These are primary witnesses to positions, not authorities replacing Genesis or Acts.
visual: Draw two aligned tracks for stated human intention and stated divine purpose in Joseph and the cross. Mark the mechanism between them as debated; never use a flowchart to imply access to God’s hidden explanation for a reader’s suffering.
caveats: Scripture supports both God’s rule and accountable action more clearly than it specifies a philosophical mechanism. The strongest starting conclusion preserves both. It does not follow that one may excuse abuse as God’s will, refuse medicine, or confidently explain another person’s tragedy.
questions: How can choices matter under providence?
What does Scripture authorize us to say about suffering?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S05 Westminster Assembly, Westminster Confession of Faith (source)
F-S09 John Wesley, Free Grace (source)

title: One God Father Son and Holy Spirit
core: The Trinity is the Christian confession that the one God eternally exists as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The doctrine gathers several biblical claims rather than quoting a single verse containing its later technical wording.
why: It explains why Christians worship Jesus, pray to the Father through the Son, and speak of the Spirit as divine without confessing three gods. It also teaches readers how a responsible doctrine can arise through synthesis.

scripture.note: Confesses Israel’s one God and undivided devotion.
Distinguishes the baptized Son, descending Spirit, and speaking Father.
Names Father, Son, and Spirit together in baptism.
Affirms the Word’s relation to God, deity, and incarnation.
Connects lying to the Holy Spirit with lying to God.

explicit: The passages affirm one God, distinguish Father and Son, identify the Word as God, and speak of the Spirit in divine terms. Matthew does not portray one person merely changing roles during Jesus' baptism.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: the classical formula of one divine being and three persons holds these statements together. The words being and person clarify a synthesis; they are not hidden translations of the singular "name" in Matthew 28.
unnoticed: Trinitarian language appears in instructions for baptism and blessing, not only in abstract debate. Second Corinthians 13:14 places communion with Father, Son, and Spirit in the life of a troubled church.
context: Historical theology: the Orthodox Church in America’s doctrinal exposition explains person and nature within the Nicene tradition. It is used as a primary witness to Orthodox formulation. It does not turn the later terminology into an explicit biblical sentence.
visual: Use a passage-first matrix: unity, personal distinction, and divine identity. Open each cell to its full passage. Avoid water, egg, or three-person analogies as explanatory proofs because they readily imply changing modes or three separate gods.
caveats: The synthesis has very strong canonical support, but classify the synthesis as inference. Do not rely on the disputed expanded wording of 1 John 5:7. Eastern and Western churches differ on the Spirit’s procession; that later disagreement requires separate historical treatment.
questions: Where do the biblical components appear?
How is the Trinity different from three gods or three roles?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S01 Orthodox Church in America, The Holy Trinity (source)

title: The Father and the Gift of Adoption
core: Jesus reveals and teaches trust in the Father. Believers are invited into a relationship of prayer, care, discipline, and inheritance through the Son and by the Spirit.
why: This makes the language of Father intelligible to newcomers without making imperfect human fathers the measure of God. It also distinguishes God’s care as Creator from the New Testament’s specific language of adoption in Christ.

scripture.note: Jesus teaches disciples to pray to their Father.
God’s giving surpasses imperfect human parental care.
Jesus speaks of his Father and the disciples' Father while preserving distinction.
The Spirit accompanies adoption, prayer, and inheritance.
Uses parental discipline to interpret formation in holiness.

explicit: Jesus calls disciples to pray for God’s name, kingdom, daily provision, forgiveness, and deliverance. Romans describes the Spirit’s witness that believers are God’s children. Hebrews presents discipline as directed toward holiness, not arbitrary punishment.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: Christian prayer participates in the Son’s relation to the Father without making believers divine in the same sense as Christ. John 20:17 says "my" and "your" rather than erasing the distinctive identity of the Son.
unnoticed: The Lord’s Prayer begins with "our," and its requests are plural. Even private prayer teaches a disciple to ask as part of a people.
context: No claim about ancient adoption law is needed for this page. Such context can enrich a later study, but Paul’s stated themes of belonging and inheritance already provide the basic meaning.
visual: Display the prayer as a sequence of shared requests. Link each request to the Father’s character and to a related practice such as forgiveness, generosity, or trust; allow readers to compare Matthew 6 with Luke 11:1-13.
caveats: God as Father does not endorse abusive parenting, and suffering must not automatically be diagnosed as punishment for a particular sin. Maternal imagery also appears in Scripture, including Isaiah 49:15; divine fatherhood is not a claim that God is biologically male.
questions: Why does Jesus teach "our Father"?
How does adoption differ from Jesus' unique sonship?

title: Why the New Testament Calls Jesus Divine
core: Jesus is presented as more than a teacher or prophet: the New Testament identifies him with divine titles, divine works, worship, and the identity of the Creator, while distinguishing him from the Father.
why: Christ’s identity determines how the gospel, worship, and salvation are understood. A passage-based study lets readers examine the evidence directly rather than being asked to accept a doctrinal slogan.

scripture.note: The Word is with God, is God, and is involved in all creation.
Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as Lord and God in the Gospel’s climactic confession.
All things are created through and for the Son; he precedes and sustains them.
The Son is distinguished from angels and receives divine and creator language.
Christ’s humiliation and exaltation culminate in universal confession of his lordship.

explicit: John calls the Word God and then identifies the incarnate Word within the narrative of Jesus. Thomas’s confession is addressed to Jesus. Hebrews contrasts the Son with servants and applies language from Psalms to him.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: these texts belong together as an account of divine identity rather than an accumulation of honorary titles. Philippians 2:10-11 echoes Isaiah 45:22-23, where universal allegiance belongs to the LORD, while directing the confession to the Father’s glory.
unnoticed: Hebrews argues for the Son’s superiority using Israel’s Scriptures. High claims about Jesus are embedded in close reading of the Old Testament, not introduced as a dismissal of it.
context: No external source is needed to state the passages' language. Later creeds articulate how deity and personal distinction fit together; those formulations should be labeled historical doctrinal synthesis.
visual: Create a claim-evidence table with titles, creation, worship, and scriptural reuse. Each row opens the full paragraph and a counter-question, so readers can test whether a title is literal, quoted, or figurative in that context.
caveats: "Firstborn" in Colossians 1:15 must be read with verses 16-17, not assumed to mean the first creature. Do not rest the case on John 1:18 alone because its wording has textual variants. Christ’s deity must be studied together with his real humanity.
questions: Which passages make the strongest claims?
How do they maintain a distinction between Jesus and the Father?

title: The Word Became Flesh
core: The incarnation is the Son’s becoming genuinely human without ceasing to be divine. Jesus' human body, growth, emotions, temptations, suffering, and death are essential to the New Testament’s account of salvation.
why: If Jesus only appeared human, his solidarity with people and his death would be emptied of meaning. This page helps readers hold together the Gospel narratives and the doctrinal claims about his identity.

scripture.note: The Word becomes flesh and reveals the Father.
Jesus grows, learns within family life, and increases in wisdom.
Shared flesh and blood relate to liberation and priestly help.
Jesus' testing and sinlessness ground confident approach for mercy.
The Son takes a servant’s condition and obeys to death.

explicit: Jesus shares flesh and blood, suffers, is tested, and dies. Luke portrays real growth. Hebrews states that his testing was without sin and connects his humanity to compassionate priestly ministry.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: the one Jesus must be confessed as truly divine and truly human. Philippians describes self-humbling through taking servant form; it does not explicitly say that Jesus discarded deity like a possession.
unnoticed: Hebrews treats shared humanity as part of why Jesus can help the tested, not as an embarrassing limitation that theology must explain away.
context: Historical theology: the Council of Chalcedon’s definition in 451 used "two natures" to protect full deity and humanity within one person. The consulted historical text records the formula; it is not itself a biblical verse or a substitute for the passages.
visual: Use two columns of textual evidence, divine identity and genuine humanity, joined to one central identity. A short historical layer can reveal later doctrinal vocabulary and the errors it was intended to exclude.
caveats: Christians debate how divine knowledge relates to human growth and sayings such as Mark 13:32. The passages establish genuine humanity more securely than they explain its psychological mechanism. Oriental Orthodox traditions also confess full deity and humanity while historically disputing Chalcedonian terminology; do not caricature them as denying either.
questions: What did Jesus share with humanity?
How can he grow and suffer while being divine?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S13 Council of Chalcedon, Definition of Faith (451) (source)

title: The Holy Spirit Gives Life and Forms a People
core: The Holy Spirit is God’s active presence giving life, revealing truth, empowering witness, and forming Christlike character. The New Testament speaks of the Spirit as a personal divine agent, not merely a religious feeling or impersonal energy.
why: This grounds everyday Christian life in God’s action while keeping spiritual experiences accountable to Scripture. It also connects the Spirit’s work across creation, Israel’s hope, Jesus' mission, and the church.

scripture.note: Promises cleansing, a new heart, and God’s Spirit enabling obedience.
Jesus promises the Spirit who teaches and remains with disciples.
The Spirit directs the setting apart and sending of Barnabas and Saul.
The Spirit gives life, leads believers, and witnesses to adoption.
Life by the Spirit produces a recognizable pattern of conduct.

explicit: The Spirit teaches, sends, leads, and gives life. Ezekiel relates the gift to renewed obedience; Galatians contrasts the Spirit’s fruit with destructive practices. These actions cannot be reduced to the intensity of an experience.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: the Spirit’s personal agency and divine identity belong together with the Father and Son. Ezekiel’s promised renewal helps explain why Pentecost is more than an isolated miracle, though Acts 2 interprets that event explicitly through Joel 2:28-32.
unnoticed: Acts 13 depicts mission arising from a community engaged in worship and fasting. Guidance is narrated within communal discernment rather than as an independent individual claim immune to testing.
context: No outside historical explanation is needed for these claims. Later debates about procession, gifts, and the timing of Spirit baptism must be kept distinct from the text’s explicit account of the Spirit’s work.
visual: Build a timeline with creation, prophetic promise, Jesus, Pentecost, and ordinary church life. Every node opens passages; a separate action filter groups teaching, empowering, sanctifying, and assuring.
caveats: The apostles receive particular promises in John 14; do not transfer every detail to every believer without argument. First John 4:1-3 commands testing of spiritual claims. The Spirit’s presence does not make a person incapable of error, illness, doubt, or the need for counsel.
questions: How does the Spirit act?
How should claimed guidance be tested?

title: Creation as Gift and Vocation
core: God is Creator, creation is his good gift, and humans are entrusted with responsible life within it. Biblical creation texts teach worship, dependence, work, rest, and care; questions of mechanism and chronology require additional interpretation.
why: Creation doctrine shapes how readers understand bodily life, the natural world, and human limits. It gives a foundational orientation without treating one reading of every disputed scientific or chronological question as the definition of Christianity.

scripture.note: God orders the world, calls it good, and gives humanity a vocation.
Work, rest, life, and limits are placed within God’s provision.
Celebrates creatures, ecological dependence, and God’s sustaining care.
All created things are made through the Word.
Creation grounds heavenly praise.

explicit: Genesis calls the created order good before narrating human disobedience. Humans receive food and a task; they do not create their own existence. Psalm 104 includes wild creatures beyond direct human usefulness in its praise.
insight: Debated interpretation: young-earth readings understand Genesis 1’s days as ordinary successive days; old-earth and evolutionary-creation readings emphasize literary organization, divine accommodation, or a distinction between theological affirmation and natural mechanism. All must account for the text’s goodness, order, and divine agency.
unnoticed: Psalm 104 praises a world that includes lions seeking prey. Its celebration of creation cannot simply be replaced by a modern picture of nature existing only for human comfort.
context: No scientific dating claim is made here. Geological, biological, and ancient cosmological questions need their own qualified sources; the doctrine of creation does not by itself calculate the earth’s age.
visual: Present Genesis 1 alongside Psalm 104 and John 1. Allow readers to compare order, provision, and praise before opening a clearly labeled interpretations panel about the days.
caveats: The strongest shared conclusion is the text’s affirmation of God as Creator and creation as good. The precise relation of the account to scientific models is debated. Do not call matter evil, use dominion to excuse destruction, or claim that the Bible supplies a modern scientific vocabulary.
questions: What does creation teach about work and dependence?
Which claims are explicit and which concern interpretation of time?

title: Every Person Bears God’s Image
core: Human beings are made in God’s image. The texts connect that status with a shared vocation under God and with the seriousness of violence and contempt toward other people.
why: This supplies a biblical basis for human dignity that does not depend on achievement, wealth, sex, ethnicity, strength, or usefulness. It also links creation doctrine to the treatment of vulnerable neighbors.

scripture.note: Male and female humanity receive image-bearing status and a vocation.
The image of God grounds the gravity of shedding human blood.
Cursing people is condemned because they are made in God’s likeness.
Renewal in the Creator’s image changes social relationships.
Transformation is described in relation to the Lord’s image.

explicit: Genesis applies the image to humanity as male and female. After the fall narrative, Genesis 9 still invokes that image. James addresses speech, not merely physical violence, as a place where this truth has ethical force.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: the image is not simply lost whenever someone behaves badly or lacks a particular ability. Relational, functional, and structural interpretations emphasize communion, representative rule, or human capacities. Genesis 1 most directly connects the image to humanity’s shared vocation.
unnoticed: James sees a contradiction between worshiping God and verbally degrading people made in his likeness. An everyday habit can contradict a foundational doctrine.
context: No comparative ancient royal ideology is necessary for this introductory page. An advanced module may compare ancient images and royal representation, but it must not make an external parallel the sole meaning of the biblical term.
visual: Create a creation-to-renewal network with three ethical branches: protection of life, speech about neighbors, and renewed community. Keep Genesis 1 and Genesis 9 visible together.
caveats: The Bible does not define the image by a single faculty such as intelligence. Such a definition can wrongly exclude infants or people with disabilities. Image-bearing does not mean people share God’s uncreated essence or that every human preference has divine authority.
questions: Is the image erased by sin?
What does this doctrine require in speech and social life?

title: Sin the Fall and the Human Predicament
core: Sin is opposition to God expressed through wrongful acts, disordered desires, failures to love, and participation in destructive patterns. Genesis portrays human distrust and disobedience; Paul connects Adam’s transgression with humanity’s condition of sin and death.
why: The gospel addresses a predicament deeper than occasional mistakes. This study explains the need for grace while resisting claims that human beings cease to have dignity or that every suffering person is guilty of some identifiable special sin.

scripture.note: Narrates disobedience, shame, blame, exile, and mortality.
Describes the universality of sin and God’s justifying gift.
Compares Adam’s trespass and Christ’s obedient saving act.
Includes failure to do known good within sin.
Describes bondage and God’s merciful life-giving response.

explicit: Genesis identifies the forbidden act but does not name the fruit as an apple. Paul presents sin and death as universal and contrasts Adam with Christ. James includes omission, not only overt wrongdoing.
insight: Debated interpretation: Western accounts of original sin often discuss inherited guilt as well as corruption; Eastern accounts commonly emphasize ancestral mortality and corruption without personal blame for Adam’s individual act. Romans 5’s Adam-Christ parallel anchors the debate; Ezekiel 18:20 guards individual accountability.
unnoticed: Genesis repeatedly depicts blaming: the man points to the woman and indirectly to God, and the woman points to the serpent. The narrative exposes relational rupture as well as rule-breaking.
context: Historical theology is needed to explain later original-sin terminology. This introductory page reports the biblical predicament first; it does not infer a biological mechanism for transmitting sin.
visual: Use a narrative sequence from command to distrust, action, hiding, blame, and exile. A parallel Romans 5 panel shows how the apostle himself relates Adam and Christ.
caveats: Human dignity persists after Genesis 3, as Genesis 9:6 shows. Christians debate inherited guilt, infant salvation, and the historical-literary reading of Adam. Do not equate disability or illness with personal wrongdoing; John 9:1-3 explicitly challenges that shortcut.
questions: Is sin only an action?
How are Adam, personal responsibility, and death related?

title: Temptation and the Reality of Resistance
core: Temptation is enticement toward unfaithfulness. Scripture distinguishes being tested from consenting to sin and portrays resistance through trust, prayer, wise action, and reliance on God’s help.
why: This prevents guilt about every unwanted thought and helps readers resist the claim that temptation proves God’s abandonment. It also gives a sober account of Satan without making him the explanation for every difficult experience.

scripture.note: The serpent distorts trust in God’s command and goodness.
Jesus resists temptation through contextual appeal to Deuteronomy.
Distinguishes God’s giving from temptation arising through desire.
Uses Israel’s failures to warn believers and affirm God’s faithfulness.
Jesus' sinless testing grounds help and mercy.

explicit: Jesus is tempted and does not sin. James says God does not entice anyone into evil. Paul warns confident believers against falling while affirming that temptation is not beyond God’s capacity to provide a faithful way through.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: resistance is not merely willpower or repeating detached verses. Jesus' quotations come from Israel’s wilderness instruction about dependence, testing God, and exclusive worship. Satan also quotes Scripture, demonstrating that citation alone does not guarantee faithful interpretation.
unnoticed: In Matthew 4 the tempter quotes a psalm. The dispute involves how Scripture is used, not a contest between one person with Bible verses and another without them.
context: No extrabiblical demonology is needed. Later stories about Satan’s hierarchy, psychology, or power must not be inserted into these texts without independent labeling.
visual: Build a side-by-side comparison of each temptation, the offered shortcut, Jesus' reply, and its Deuteronomy context. Link to Israel’s corresponding wilderness episodes.
caveats: First Corinthians 10:13 concerns temptation and faithfulness; it does not promise that every burden of suffering will feel manageable. Second Corinthians 1:8-9 describes affliction beyond Paul’s strength. Unwanted intrusive thoughts should not be equated automatically with chosen sin.
questions: Is being tempted itself sin?
How does Jesus use Scripture differently from the tempter?

title: The Cross in the Gospel Narratives
core: Jesus is crucified under Roman authority, dies, and is buried. The Gospels interpret these events through kingship, obedience, Scripture, forgiveness, and the response of witnesses.
why: The cross is central to the gospel but can become an abstract symbol detached from the narratives. Reading the accounts closely allows doctrine to grow from what the texts actually narrate.

scripture.note: Narrates mockery, crucifixion, death, the torn curtain, and burial.
Highlights lament, innocence, a condemned man’s appeal, and witnesses.
Links the execution with Scripture, completion, and testimony.
Interprets the cross as God’s wisdom amid human expectations.
Places death on a cross within Christ’s self-humbling and exaltation.

explicit: The narratives identify Roman execution and name Joseph of Arimathea in the burial accounts. They portray mockery of Jesus' kingship, his death, and varied reactions. Paul calls the crucified Christ central to his proclamation.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: the irony of royal mockery matters. The figure ridiculed as king is confessed by Christians as Lord. Mark’s torn curtain and centurion’s response invite interpretation, but the narrative should be read before assigning a complete symbolic system to every detail.
unnoticed: In Mark, a Roman centurion’s confession follows Jesus' death. Recognition comes from an unexpected observer at the point that appears to defeat messianic expectations.
context: Historical context - not explicitly stated in Scripture: reconstructing Roman execution procedures requires ancient evidence. This page does not repeat uncertain medical claims, exact nail placement, or sensational estimates of suffering.
visual: Use four Gospel columns aligned by narrated event, with differences preserved. Let users expand each account’s scriptural references and distinguish reported sequence from a proposed combined chronology.
caveats: Do not attribute collective guilt to Jewish people; the texts include varied Jewish actors and Roman authority, and Christian doctrine applies sin universally. The exact calendar date is debated. Do not build an interpretation on Luke 23:34 without noting that the prayer’s first sentence has a textual variant.
questions: What does each Gospel emphasize?
How does royal mockery contribute to the meaning of the cross?

title: How the New Testament Explains Atonement
core: Atonement names Christ’s saving work in dealing with sin and restoring communion with God. The New Testament uses several connected images: sacrifice, reconciliation, ransom, victory, representation, substitution, and example.
why: One image alone can flatten the Bible’s account. This study helps readers recognize how different passages address guilt, alienation, bondage, death, and transformed life without pretending that all Christian theories are identical.

scripture.note: Relates Christ’s blood to righteousness, faith, and God’s dealing with sin.
Connects Christ’s death with representation, new creation, and reconciliation.
Jesus describes his self-giving as a ransom and grounds servant leadership in it.
Joins forgiveness, canceled debt, and triumph over powers.
Combines example, bearing sins, healing, and return to the shepherd.

explicit: The texts explicitly connect Christ’s death with sins, reconciliation, liberation, and victory. First Peter includes both an example to follow and sin-bearing; separating those into mutually exclusive biblical messages misreads the paragraph.
insight: Debated interpretation: penal-substitution accounts emphasize judgment borne for sinners; Christus Victor emphasizes deliverance from death and powers; satisfaction accounts emphasize restored order and obedience; moral-influence accounts emphasize love transforming human response. A robust synthesis should account for all the cited texts, rather than selecting one image as exhaustive.
unnoticed: Colossians 2 places cancellation of debt and defeat of powers in the same movement. Legal and victory language are neighbors in the text.
context: Historical theology: later atonement theories organize biblical imagery. Their familiar labels are not all names the biblical authors used for complete systems. Claims about particular medieval or modern authors require reading their works separately.
visual: Create a multi-entry diagram with the human predicament on one side and the relevant biblical image on the other. Every connection opens a paragraph and displays where the image stops explaining.
caveats: The strongest conclusion is Christ’s decisive saving self-giving, with several complementary biblical descriptions. Debate remains over mechanism, scope, and how images fit together. Do not depict the Father as unwilling to forgive until a loving Son changes his mind: 2 Corinthians 5:19 locates reconciliation in God’s own action in Christ.
questions: What problems does the cross address?
Which biblical images can be held together?

title: The Resurrection at the Center of Christian Hope
core: The New Testament proclaims that God raised Jesus from the dead. His resurrection is the vindication of the crucified Messiah, the basis of apostolic witness, and the beginning of the promised resurrection of those who belong to him.
why: The resurrection is not an optional illustration of hope. Paul explicitly makes the truth of Christian proclamation and future resurrection depend on it, giving readers a clear sense of its doctrinal importance.

scripture.note: Narrates the empty tomb, appearances, bodily recognition, and scriptural explanation.
Connects appearances with belief and the purpose of the Gospel.
Peter proclaims God’s raising and exaltation of Jesus.
Lists appearances and argues that Christ’s resurrection grounds Christian hope.
Connects resurrection with new life for believers.

explicit: Paul says that without Christ’s resurrection preaching and faith are empty and believers remain in their sins. Luke portrays Jesus as recognizable and bodily, while the narratives also describe unusual features of risen life.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: resurrection differs from merely continuing as a memory or from a temporary return to mortal life. First Corinthians 15:20-28 presents Christ as the beginning of a larger victory over death, not an isolated exception.
unnoticed: Paul treats resurrection as a premise with consequences that can be challenged. His argument explicitly considers what would follow if it had not happened.
context: Historical investigation of testimony, burial, and alternative explanations is a separate evidential task. The biblical summary here describes the texts' claims without pretending that citing them alone resolves every question of historical method.
visual: Link the narrated appearances to an argument map of 1 Corinthians 15: proclamation, counterfactual, firstfruits, and final victory. Keep disputed ordering of appearances visibly separate from the theological claims.
caveats: The Gospels do not supply a single effortless combined sequence. Some appearances listed by Paul are not narrated elsewhere. Preserve those limits rather than inventing missing scenes. Bodily resurrection does not mean that every property of present mortal life remains unchanged.
questions: Why does Paul make resurrection indispensable?
What do the accounts affirm about continuity and transformation?

title: Ascension Enthronement and Ongoing Intercession
core: The ascension is Jesus' being taken into heaven and exalted at the Father’s right hand. The New Testament connects it with his reign, the gift of the Spirit, and his continuing priestly intercession.
why: Christian retellings often jump from Easter to the Second Coming. This study explains why the New Testament treats the ascended Christ’s present ministry as a source of assurance and a basis for mission.

scripture.note: Jesus blesses the disciples and is taken into heaven.
Places the ascension after resurrection appearances and before empowered witness.
Uses Psalm 110 to explain exaltation and the Spirit’s outpouring.
Connects Christ’s enduring priesthood with intercession.
Describes Christ appearing before God on behalf of his people.

explicit: Acts says Jesus was taken from the disciples' sight and directs them toward witness and promised return. Hebrews says his priesthood continues and his self-offering is not repeatedly renewed.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: royal and priestly images converge in the exalted Jesus. Acts 2’s use of Psalm 110 and Hebrews' sanctuary language illuminate distinct aspects of the same present significance, rather than competing locations on a literal cosmic map.
unnoticed: The disciples in Luke return with joy after Jesus' departure. The story presents the event as blessing and fulfillment rather than simple loss.
context: Historical theology: Orthodox exposition relates ascension to humanity’s participation in divine life, often called theosis. This is an interpretive synthesis, informed by passages such as 2 Peter 1:4, not a claim that humans become uncreated gods.
visual: Draw connected panels for exaltation, Spirit, intercession, and witness. Each panel shows its primary text and a "what this image explains" note; avoid speculative diagrams locating heaven within outer space.
caveats: "Right hand" expresses honor and authority in these texts; the phrase should not force an anatomical account of God. Hebrews emphasizes one effective offering. Traditions debate how this relates to eucharistic sacrifice, a question that belongs in the Communion comparison.
questions: What is Christ doing now?
Why does his departure lead to mission and joy?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S08 Orthodox Church in America, The Ascension of Christ (source)

title: Grace That Saves and Teaches
core: Grace is God’s generous favor and action toward people who cannot establish a claim to salvation by their own merit. In the New Testament grace also empowers service and trains believers in a changed way of life.
why: Grace is easily reduced either to leniency about wrongdoing or to a first step after which people must save themselves. Reading its saving and formative dimensions together clarifies Christian dependence and responsibility.

scripture.note: God’s mercy gives life and salvation as gift, leading to prepared good works.
Justification is freely given through Christ rather than earned by boasting.
Grace trains believers toward godliness and hope.
Paul attributes his apostolic labor to God’s grace.
Grace sustains Paul amid weakness rather than removing every difficulty.

explicit: Ephesians denies that salvation is a ground for boasting and immediately speaks of good works. Titus says grace instructs people to renounce ungodliness. Paul describes strenuous work and persistent weakness within grace.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: grace and meaningful effort are compatible when effort is understood as response and enablement rather than purchase. First Corinthians 15:10 deliberately holds together Paul’s labor and God’s grace at work with him.
unnoticed: Titus gives grace the role of a teacher. The same grace that brings salvation trains ordinary conduct while believers await Christ.
context: Primary doctrinal context: Catholic teaching on grace and justification explicitly locates the beginning of salvation in God’s initiative. The Catholic-Lutheran Joint Declaration likewise rejects salvation as self-earned; it records agreement with continuing differences, not a merger of every doctrine.
visual: Use a sequence showing divine gift, receiving faith, and resulting life, with loops for ongoing dependence. Attach Titus 2 beside Ephesians 2 so users do not stop the discussion at the exclusion of boasting.
caveats: Christians disagree about irresistible and resistible grace, sacramental means, and the relation between justification and sanctification. Represent those disputes fairly. "Grace" does not promise financial success, freedom from illness, or permission to harm others without repentance.
questions: Can effort coexist with grace?
Does grace change behavior as well as status?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S03 Catholic Church, Catechism of the Catholic Church: Grace and Justification (source)
F-S10 Lutheran World Federation and Catholic Church, Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (2019) (source)

title: Faith as Trust That Becomes Visible
core: Faith is reliance on God and his promise, centered for Christians on Jesus Christ. Scripture distinguishes living trust from a bare claim of belief that leaves conduct untouched.
why: Faith can be confused with optimism, certainty about a desired outcome, or intellectual agreement alone. The biblical examples show trust directed toward a trustworthy God and expressed through responsive action.

scripture.note: Abram believes God’s promise amid an unresolved future.
Paul interprets Abraham’s trust apart from wages or prior circumcision.
Challenges a claimed faith that withholds necessary help.
Describes trust expressed through obedience without immediate possession of promises.
Connects faith with love rather than boundary-marking achievement.

explicit: Paul distinguishes receiving a promise from earning wages. James asks whether an unproductive claim to faith can save and illustrates the problem through unmet bodily needs. Hebrews depicts faithful people acting without seeing full fulfillment.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: Romans and James address different distortions. Paul denies grounds for boasting before God; James denies that a verbal profession without deeds is living faith. Their common Abraham example should be read in the different narrative stages they invoke.
unnoticed: Paul emphasizes Genesis 15 before circumcision; James invokes Abraham’s later offering of Isaac. The sequence matters for understanding what each argument is doing.
context: No special Greek definition settles the theological debate. The range of pistis must be examined in context; a word can concern trust, faithfulness, or a body of belief in different settings.
visual: Create a timeline of Abraham’s story with Romans 4 and James 2 as distinct interpretive lenses. A question panel asks what each writer opposes and what he commends.
caveats: Christians disagree about justification’s relation to transformed life, but neither writer commends empty profession or self-earned salvation. Do not define strong faith as never having questions; Mark 9:24 portrays an appeal for help with unbelief.
questions: What distinguishes trust from mere assent?
Are Paul and James addressing the same problem?

title: Repentance More Than Regret
core: Repentance is a turning toward God that includes recognition of wrongdoing and a changed direction of life. Scripture associates it with God’s kindness, forgiveness, and fruits appropriate to that turning.
why: Regret can concern being caught or suffering consequences without concern for the wrong itself. This study helps readers distinguish emotional intensity, honest confession, concrete repair, and enduring change.

scripture.note: John calls for fruit and gives concrete examples involving goods, wages, and power.
The younger son returns and is received while the older son is challenged.
Peter connects turning back with forgiveness and restoration.
God’s kindness aims toward repentance rather than complacency.
Distinguishes kinds of sorrow by their resulting response.

explicit: John’s hearers are told to share clothing and food, collect honestly, and reject extortion. Paul distinguishes sorrow that leads to repentance from sorrow that produces death. Peter’s appeal includes forgiveness, not merely condemnation.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: repentance has moral direction rather than one compulsory emotional style. The return of the younger son cannot be reduced to perfect motives, and the father’s welcome does not make the earlier wastefulness good.
unnoticed: John answers different occupations with different practical obligations. Repentance is observable in how people use their particular responsibilities and advantages.
context: No etymological claim that repentance "only means changing your mind" can replace these contexts. The passage’s actions and consequences determine the meaning more reliably than dividing a Greek word into its parts.
visual: Build a response map connecting wrongdoing, confession, turning, repair where possible, and ongoing fruit. Let readers compare John’s concrete examples with the Corinthian church’s response.
caveats: Repentance does not purchase mercy through sufficient distress. Nor does forgiveness automatically restore every lost role or relationship. A person’s sorrow should not be measured by public display alone; Scripture’s concern is truth and changed direction.
questions: How does repentance differ from shame?
What fruit would fit a particular wrong?

title: Justification and Peace with God
core: Justification concerns being set right before God through Christ. Paul connects it with grace, faith, forgiveness, and peace; traditions disagree about how its declarative and transformative dimensions should be distinguished.
why: This is a central doctrine for understanding salvation and a major place where Christians talk past one another. Close comparison lets readers see both shared affirmations and the remaining interpretive disagreements.

scripture.note: God justifies through Christ, excluding boasting and ethnic restriction.
Abraham and David illustrate credited righteousness and forgiveness.
Justification brings peace, hope, and reconciliation.
Rejects a dead profession of faith without deeds.
Joins mercy, renewal, justification, inheritance, and good works.

explicit: Paul says justification is freely given by grace and received through faith apart from works of law. James says a faith that produces no action is dead. Titus describes salvation through mercy and immediately calls for useful good works.
insight: Debated interpretation: Reformed and Lutheran accounts distinguish God’s favorable verdict from the renewal that follows it; Catholic accounts include forgiveness and inward renewal within justification; Orthodox accounts often frame the whole saving life as healing and participation. Romans 4 strongly supports gift and non-boasting; James 2 requires living, active faith.
unnoticed: Romans 3 moves directly from justification to the question whether God belongs to Jews alone. The doctrine has implications for who belongs in one people, not only for an individual conscience.
context: Primary tradition sources: Catholic Catechism 1987-1995 and the Catholic-Lutheran Joint Declaration describe the disputed terminology and shared dependence on grace. They are witnesses to those positions, not substitutes for exegesis.
visual: Create a comparison matrix of biblical text, question addressed, and each tradition’s interpretation. Display common ground first, then clarify which terms have different definitions.
caveats: Editorial judgment: any adequate account must preserve unearned grace and the necessity of living faith. The precise relation of verdict and renewal remains debated. Avoid the caricature that Catholics teach salvation earned without grace or Protestants teach that transformed life is irrelevant.
questions: What is credited righteousness?
Why do Christians use the same word differently?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S03 Catholic Church, Catechism of the Catholic Church: Grace and Justification (source)
F-S10 Lutheran World Federation and Catholic Church, Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (2019) (source)

title: New Birth and the Renewal God Gives
core: Regeneration or new birth is God’s gift of new life. Jesus says that entry into God’s kingdom requires birth from above; apostolic texts connect renewal with the Spirit, mercy, faith, and God’s living word.
why: This explains why Christianity speaks about more than better habits or ancestry. It also gives a careful starting point for debates about baptism and the relation between divine initiative and human response.

scripture.note: Jesus speaks to Nicodemus about birth from above, water and Spirit, and belief.
Promises cleansing, a new heart, and the Spirit.
Locates washing and renewal in divine mercy rather than righteous works.
Connects new birth with God’s enduring word and mutual love.
God brings people forth through the word of truth.

explicit: Jesus insists on a birth that human ancestry cannot supply. Titus attributes renewal to mercy and the Spirit. First Peter places the resulting life within sincere love for others.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: Ezekiel’s cleansing and Spirit promise is a strong background for John 3, especially Jesus' expectation that Israel’s teacher should understand. Baptismal readings emphasize water and Spirit with Titus 3; non-sacramental readings emphasize prophetic cleansing and the surrounding call to faith.
unnoticed: The Greek term in John 3:3 can mean again or from above. Nicodemus’s misunderstanding and John 3:31 make the double sense useful rather than a secret alternate doctrine.
context: Linguistic context: the consulted NET note on John 3:3 explicitly discusses the double meaning and cites lexical evidence. This supports the limited word observation, not a complete theory of the order of salvation.
visual: Use John 3 as an annotated conversation. Open Ezekiel 36 beside the water-Spirit saying, and offer a separate comparison of baptismal and cleansing readings.
caveats: Reformed traditions often place regeneration logically before saving faith; Arminian traditions stress enabling grace and faith in receiving new life; sacramental traditions connect regeneration closely with baptism. John 3 establishes the need for God-given life more directly than it settles every later sequence. Compare whole paragraphs.
questions: What does "born again" mean in context?
How do water, Spirit, word, and faith relate?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S14 NET Bible editorial team, NET Bible Notes: John 3:3 (source)

title: Adoption Belonging and Inheritance
core: Adoption is the believer’s reception into God’s family through Christ. Paul uses it to speak of present belonging, freedom to approach the Father, shared inheritance, and the future redemption of the body.
why: This deepens a view of salvation limited to cancellation of guilt. Believers are welcomed into a relationship and a people, and the promised future includes bodily life rather than only an inward sense of acceptance.

scripture.note: The sending of Son and Spirit changes slavery into filial belonging.
Connects adoption with the Spirit, suffering, inheritance, and future bodily redemption.
Places adoption within God’s purpose in Christ.
Those who receive the Word are given the right to become God’s children.

explicit: Paul says believers can call God Father through the Spirit. He also says they await adoption understood as the redemption of their bodies. Present belonging and future fulfillment coexist in Romans 8.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: salvation has an already-present and still-awaited dimension. Adoption links assurance with hope rather than guaranteeing freedom from hardship. Romans 8:17 expressly joins heirship with suffering alongside Christ.
unnoticed: Paul can describe adoption as both possessed and awaited within one chapter. The apparent tension becomes intelligible when belonging and its full bodily inheritance are distinguished.
context: Ancient adoption law can offer context, but no claim about a universal Roman legal procedure is necessary here. The theological meaning should first be established from Paul’s own explanation.
visual: Create two linked panels labeled present belonging and future inheritance. Let each occurrence of adoption in Romans 8 light up the relevant panel and show how suffering fits between them.
caveats: The language of sons in inheritance contexts should not exclude women; Galatians 3:26-29 explicitly includes male and female in belonging to Christ. Adoption does not erase Christ’s distinctive sonship or make believers divine by nature.
questions: How can adoption be both present and future?
Why does inheritance coexist with suffering?

title: Life in Christ and the Shape of Union
core: Union with Christ describes believers' participation in his life and saving work. The New Testament speaks of being in Christ, abiding in him, belonging to his body, and sharing the pattern of his death and resurrection.
why: This connects doctrines that can otherwise look like disconnected benefits. Forgiveness, holiness, fellowship, and hope are related to a living relationship with Christ rather than a collection of independent religious achievements.

scripture.note: The vine-and-branches image joins abiding, fruit, prayer, and love.
Union with Christ’s death and resurrection grounds a new way of life.
Paul describes living by faith in the Son who loved and gave himself.
One body contains diverse members who need one another.
Shared life in Christ grounds putting away vice and practicing communal virtues.

explicit: Jesus commands abiding and love. Paul argues that those joined to Christ must not continue treating sin as their master. The body image makes mutual need and care explicit.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: union is both personal and communal. John’s vine image, Paul’s body image, and the death-resurrection pattern overlap without being identical. No single metaphor supplies a complete physical mechanism for how participation occurs.
unnoticed: First Corinthians 12 gives special care to members judged weaker. Union with Christ changes how importance is assigned within the community.
context: Historical theology: traditions describe participation through sacramental, covenantal, and mystical language. Orthodox theosis emphasizes sharing divine life by grace; it does not mean dissolving the human person into God’s essence.
visual: Build a metaphor explorer with vine, body, and death-to-life views. The selected image shows only the relations the passage supports and offers a clear boundary for what must not be inferred.
caveats: Abiding is not passivity, and communion is not loss of personal identity. Christians debate the interpretation of the cut-off branches in John 15 and the sacramental dimensions of Romans 6. The strongest shared conclusion joins dependence on Christ to practical love and holiness.
questions: How does being in Christ change conduct?
What does each metaphor illuminate?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S18 Church of England, The Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion (source)

title: Sanctification and Growth in Holiness
core: Sanctification is being set apart for God and being transformed in life. Scripture can speak of believers as already sanctified and also call them to pursue holiness and grow in love.
why: This helps readers understand why Christians still need repentance and formation. It also prevents growth from becoming either a self-salvation project or an excuse to accept destructive patterns as inevitable.

scripture.note: Addresses a troubled church as sanctified in Christ.
Calls believers to increasing holiness, sexual integrity, and love.
Joins active obedience with God’s action in willing and doing.
Connects sanctification with Christ’s effective offering.
Describes ongoing transformation by the Spirit.

explicit: Paul calls imperfect Corinthians sanctified and then corrects their conduct. Thessalonians are urged to abound more and more. Philippians places God’s enabling work underneath the command to work out salvation.
insight: Debated interpretation: Reformed and Lutheran traditions stress lifelong struggle with sin; Wesleyan traditions stress the possibility of entire sanctification or mature perfect love. The latter need not mean infallibility or freedom from every human limitation. First Thessalonians 5:23-24 and 1 John 1:8-10 belong in the comparison.
unnoticed: The address to "sanctified" Corinthians comes before the letter’s rebukes about factions and exploitation. A given identity becomes the reason to change, not evidence that no change is needed.
context: Primary tradition context: Methodist doctrinal materials describe sanctification as grace-enabled renewal and wholehearted love. This is evidence for Wesleyan self-description, not an independent proof that one account exhausts every biblical use.
visual: Draw a two-axis study: status in Christ and developing conduct. Attach each passage to the dimension it emphasizes; add a comparison panel for growth and perfection language.
caveats: Editorial judgment: the texts clearly teach God-enabled growth and continuing need for confession. They require more argument to establish a particular crisis experience as universal. Holiness must be evaluated through love, truth, justice, and self-control, not only a group’s external markers.
questions: Why are imperfect believers called holy?
What does Christian perfection mean in different traditions?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S04 The United Methodist Church, Articles of Religion (source)

title: Assurance Without Pretending to Be Perfect
core: Assurance is confidence in God’s saving promise and present relationship with him. Scripture locates it in Christ, the Spirit’s witness, and the recognizable life of trust and love while warning against empty profession.
why: Readers need confidence that does not depend on constantly measuring the strength of their feelings. They also need to distinguish comfort grounded in Christ from a claim that religious words make conduct irrelevant.

scripture.note: Jesus describes his sheep, his gift of life, and his protecting care.
The Spirit, Christ’s intercession, and God’s love ground confidence amid suffering.
Christ advocates for sinners while claims to know him are tested by conduct.
Practical love relates to confidence before God.
The letter states its purpose of encouraging knowledge of eternal life.

explicit: First John addresses people so they may know that they have life. It also rejects the claim of sinlessness in 1 John 1:8-10 and points to Christ’s advocacy. Romans locates confidence amid distress rather than in the absence of it.
insight: Strong scriptural inference: assurance combines looking to God’s promise with honest attention to the direction of life. The tests in First John concern allegiance, truth, and love; they are not a command to achieve flawless behavior before trusting mercy.
unnoticed: The same letter that encourages assurance says believers deceive themselves if they claim to have no sin. Its confidence is compatible with confession.
context: Historical theology: Westminster Confession chapter 18 distinguishes saving faith from uninterrupted subjective certainty. Other traditions relate assurance differently to perseverance and sacramental life. No personality style should be made a theological requirement.
visual: Create a reading path that alternates promise, evidence of life, and response to failure. Keep Christ’s advocacy visible when readers open a warning passage.
caveats: Assurance and perseverance are related but distinct questions. Do not diagnose another person’s eternal destiny from a brief exchange or treat every doubt as unbelief. Conversely, biblical confidence does not excuse ongoing exploitation or refusal to repent.
questions: Can a believer have doubts?
What is the difference between assurance and presumption?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S05 Westminster Assembly, Westminster Confession of Faith (source)

title: Perseverance and the Warning Passages
core: Perseverance concerns continuing in faith to the end. Scripture gives strong promises of God’s preserving care and serious warnings against abandoning Christ; Christians dispute how these relate to the final salvation of a once-believing person.
why: This debate affects preaching, assurance, and care for people who fail. The study should keep promises and warnings together, allowing neither a careless presumption nor an interpretation that removes every ground for hope.

scripture.note: Jesus promises life and protection to his sheep.
God’s saving purpose and love sustain confidence.
Warns about falling away and then expresses hope for the readers.
Pairs confident access with a severe warning and a call to endurance.
Interprets the departure of opponents and urges abiding.

explicit: Hebrews does not present its warnings as trivia: it calls readers to hold fast, encourage one another, and endure. John 10 affirms Christ’s protection. First John describes a particular departure as exposing a lack of true belonging.
insight: Debated interpretation: Reformed readings take final apostasy as evidence of non-saving participation or understand warnings as means God uses to preserve the elect. Wesleyan-Arminian readings take warnings as real possibilities for genuine believers. Some Free Grace readings interpret particular warnings as loss of reward or temporal judgment; the destruction language presents them a substantial challenge.
unnoticed: Hebrews 6 follows its warning with confidence in the readers' better response and then an anchor image of hope. The pastoral movement includes both alarm and encouragement.
context: Primary tradition sources: Westminster chapter 17 and Baptist Faith and Message article V affirm final perseverance; Methodist article XII allows departure from grace and restoration. These establish representative positions, not uniformity within every denomination.
visual: Build a side-by-side argument map in which every view must explain the same five passage units. Distinguish a view’s direct textual observations from its harmonizing inference.
caveats: Editorial judgment: perseverance is necessary and God’s keeping is powerful; the texts should not be used to trivialize either. The logical reconciliation remains disputed. Hebrews' warning against repudiating Christ should not be equated with every lapse or unwanted thought.
questions: What do the warnings address?
How can promises and warnings be read together?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S02 Southern Baptist Convention, The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (source)
F-S04 The United Methodist Church, Articles of Religion (source)
F-S05 Westminster Assembly, Westminster Confession of Faith (source)

title: Election Predestination and the Purpose of Grace
core: Election is God’s choosing; predestination concerns his purpose for a people in Christ. Scripture uses these themes to speak about grace, holiness, adoption, conformity to Christ, and God’s faithfulness to his promises.
why: This topic often becomes a contest over an abstract system before its biblical purposes are heard. Reading the passages in context shows why election should cultivate gratitude, humility, mission, and trust.

scripture.note: Describes choosing in Christ, adoption, redemption, and praise.
Names conformity to the Son as the purpose of predestination.
Defends God’s faithfulness and freedom in the argument about Israel.
Warns Gentiles against arrogance and ends in praise.
Joins election, the Spirit, obedience, and guarded inheritance.

explicit: Ephesians connects election to holiness and adoption, not a license for pride. Romans 8 specifies likeness to Christ as the goal. Romans 11 directly warns Gentile believers not to boast over Israel.
insight: Debated interpretation: Calvinist readings emphasize unconditional personal election, especially Romans 9 and Ephesians 1. Arminian readings emphasize foreknowledge, grace-enabled faith, and universal saving invitation, using Romans 8:29 and 1 Timothy 2:3-6. Corporate-election readings emphasize the chosen people in Christ and the plural language of Ephesians. Each must explain both divine initiative and the texts' calls to faith.
unnoticed: The predestined destination explicitly named in Romans 8:29 is conformity to the Son. The passage is not simply a list of who goes where after death.
context: Primary historical witnesses: Westminster Confession chapter 3 articulates a Reformed synthesis; Wesley’s Free Grace argues from universal grace against unconditional reprobation. Read each as an advocate, not a neutral account of the opponent.
visual: Create a purpose-centered map linking choice to adoption, holiness, Christlikeness, mission, and praise. Add parallel argument columns for the disputed mechanisms rather than drawing one causal chain as settled fact.
caveats: Editorial judgment: grace precedes boasting and election has a Christ-centered purpose; those claims are strongest. The precise relationship of foreknowledge, freedom, and decree remains debated. Do not infer a person’s hidden election or reprobation, and do not turn Romans 9-11 into contempt for Jews.
questions: Chosen for what?
How does the Israel context shape Romans 9?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S05 Westminster Assembly, Westminster Confession of Faith (source)
F-S09 John Wesley, Free Grace (source)

title: Baptism and Belonging to Christ
core: Christian baptism is the commanded water rite associated with discipleship, repentance, forgiveness, union with Christ, and entry into the community. Its relation to the reception of grace is interpreted differently across Christian traditions.
why: The topic should begin with the range of biblical statements rather than a denominational definition alone. Readers can then see why baptism matters and why Christians disagree about language such as sign, means of grace, and regeneration.

scripture.note: Jesus commands baptism within making and teaching disciples.
Repentance, baptism, forgiveness, Spirit, and communal life appear together.
Baptism is connected with Christ’s death and new life.
Burial and resurrection in baptism are related to faith in God’s action.
Baptism is related to salvation through Jesus' resurrection, with an explicit qualification about bodily washing.

explicit: The texts command baptism and give it theological significance. First Peter denies that the saving point is ordinary removal of dirt. Colossians names faith in God’s action rather than treating the ritual as independent magic.
insight: Debated interpretation: Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran readings emphasize baptism as God’s effective gift, appealing to Acts 2:38, Titus 3:5, and 1 Peter 3:21. Baptist readings emphasize obedient testimony to prior faith and appeal to narrative sequences and the distinction from external washing. Reformed readings speak of a covenant sign and seal, distinguishing its administration from automatic saving efficacy.
unnoticed: Peter’s baptism passage ends with the risen and exalted Jesus, not with water considered in isolation. Its logic centers on Christ’s saving victory.
context: Primary confessional witnesses: the Augsburg Confession article IX and Baptist Faith and Message article VII offer contrasting accounts. Their authority here is representative self-description.
visual: Use a passage matrix with command, meaning, response, and community columns. Add tradition overlays while keeping the same passages visible to every reader.
caveats: Editorial judgment: baptism is commanded and Christ-centered, with rich saving associations. The exact relation between sign, faith, and grace requires synthesis and remains disputed. Do not equate sacramental theology with magic or symbolic theology with the claim that baptism is unimportant.
questions: What do the passages connect with baptism?
How do traditions interpret its saving language?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S02 Southern Baptist Convention, The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (source)
F-S11 Lutheran Confessions, Augsburg Confession: Of Baptism (source)

title: Who Should Be Baptized
core: Compare believer’s baptism with the baptism of infants within Christian households. The debate turns on how the new covenant, faith, household narratives, and continuity with Israel should be related.
why: Many readers inherit a practice without understanding its biblical argument. This study gives each position its strongest case and identifies where the record does not provide the precise information interpreters would like.

scripture.note: Connects response to the message with baptism and mentions the promise for children.
Lydia and her household are baptized without a list of ages.
The jailer’s household hears the word and receives baptism.
Relates circumcision imagery and baptism in Christ.
Circumcision includes infants within Abraham’s covenant household.

explicit: Acts records household baptisms but does not explicitly identify an infant in the cited households. Genesis explicitly includes infant males in circumcision. Colossians relates circumcision and baptism while also mentioning faith in God’s action.
insight: Debated interpretation: Baptists emphasize disciple-making and narrated believing before baptism. Reformed paedobaptists emphasize covenant continuity, household inclusion, and Acts 2:39. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Methodist practices also include infants but explain grace, faith, and church membership with different theological emphases; they should not be collapsed into one argument.
unnoticed: The same household narratives are used by opposing positions because the text names the social unit without giving every member’s age or individual response.
context: Primary tradition witnesses: Catholic Catechism 1246-1255 explains infant baptism as divine gift and formation within faith; Methodist articles retain infant baptism; Baptist article VII specifies immersion of a believer.
visual: Create a comparison table with explicit statements, unstated details, and inferred covenant principles. Include a timeline of Genesis 17, prophetic covenant promises, and Acts without assuming that continuity or discontinuity is automatic.
caveats: Editorial judgment: adult converts' baptism is explicit; infant inclusion or exclusion rests on broader theological inference because household ages are unstated. That observation does not itself decide which inference is strongest. Baptismal mode is a related but separate question; avoid inferring exact water depth from every narrative.
questions: What do household baptisms prove?
Does covenant continuity include the same recipients?
SOURCE NOTES
F-S02 Southern Baptist Convention, The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (source)
F-S04 The United Methodist Church, Articles of Religion (source)
F-S12 Catholic Church, Catechism: Baptism (source)

title: The Lord’s Supper Remembrance and Participation
core: The Lord’s Supper is the meal Jesus instituted with bread and cup, related to his body, blood, new covenant, and coming kingdom. Paul describes remembrance, proclamation, participation, and responsibility toward the gathered body.
why: This central Christian practice is both unifying and disputed. Its biblical setting exposes an often-neglected connection between eucharistic theology and how the church treats poor or excluded members.

scripture.note: Jesus relates the meal to his self-giving and the new covenant.
Participation in Christ excludes participation in idolatrous worship.
The institution is recounted while rebuking division and humiliation of the poor.
Promises a new covenant characterized by knowing God and forgiveness.

explicit: Paul says the meal proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes. He condemns an assembly in which one is hungry while another is drunk. Participation and remembrance are both present in the text.
insight: Debated interpretation: Catholics teach a change of substance and sacramental presence of the one sacrifice; Orthodox affirm real participation in Christ as mystery; Lutherans affirm the true presence and distribution of body and blood; Reformed traditions emphasize spiritual feeding by faith; many Baptists emphasize memorial proclamation. Each appeals to the institution words and Paul’s participation language.
unnoticed: The practical instruction concluding Paul’s rebuke is to wait for one another. The discussion of the body cannot be detached from the treatment of the assembled community.
context: Primary tradition documents consulted: Catholic Catechism on sacrificial memorial and presence, Augsburg Confession article X, Orthodox exposition, Anglican article XXVIII, and Baptist article VII. These establish positions without deciding exegesis by institutional authority.
